keyVerseText: Unto the woman he said, I will greatly multiply thy sorrow and thy conception; in sorrow thou shalt bring forth children; and thy desire shall be to thy husband, and he shall rule over thee. to thy: or, subject to thy husband
rootMeaning: The Hebrew noun תְּשׁוּקָה (tᵉshûwqâh) derives from the root שׁוּק (shûwq), which originally conveys the idea of stretching out or reaching after something, often with the sense of abundance or overflowing. This root imagery suggests a strong, active yearning or craving, not merely a passive feeling. Thus, the literal sense of תְּשׁוּקָה enriches the common English gloss of "desire" by emphasizing an intense, almost urgent longing that stretches toward its object.
usageInScripture: The word תְּשׁוּקָה appears three times in Scripture, consistently translated with the notion of desire or longing. It is used variously to describe the woman's longing for her husband (Genesis 3:16), a man's desire for his woman (Song 7:11), and figuratively the beast's craving to devour (Genesis 4:7). These usages reveal a spectrum of desire from human relational longing to more instinctual craving, showing the word's flexibility yet underlying unity in expressing a compelling, driving yearning.
theologicalSignificance: Understanding תְּשׁוּקָה as a deep, stretching desire enriches our grasp of human relationships and the effects of the Fall. It highlights that desire is not merely emotional but is woven into the created order as a powerful force, whether in marital love or in more fallen, distorted forms. In the Christian faith, this word points us to the profound God-ordained bond between husband and wife, while also reminding us of the consequences of sin that affect these desires. Christ's redemptive work restores what was marred, offering healing to the disordered longings of the human heart and renewing the true meaning of desire within covenant relationships.
keyVerseReflection: In Genesis 3:16, God declares to the woman, "thy desire shall be to thy husband, and he shall rule over thee." Here, תְּשׁוּקָה conveys a compelling longing or yearning toward the husband, underscoring the relational dynamic established in the Fall. This desire is not neutral but tied to the sorrow and struggle introduced by sin, reflecting both a bond and a tension within marriage. The word's original meaning deepens our understanding of this verse by highlighting the intensity and complexity of the woman's longing amid a fallen context.
